findings.location: design.md#Decision: Customers are merged by e-mail
findings.recommendation: The whole plan depends on "an e-mail address identifies exactly one person", which nothing verifies and which the Context section refutes: "Business customers often share a purchasing mailbox (`orders@acme.example`) between several buyers, each with their own customer record and billing address." Failing scenario: three buyers at Acme share `orders@acme.example`; the nightly job folds them into the oldest record, deletes the other two with their billing addresses, and attributes every buyer's orders to one person — the plan builds the wrong thing. It also merges beyond the Why, which is only about guest checkouts creating a new record each time (the release note says the same), while the requirement merges every customer sharing an e-mail. Choose a key that holds for shared mailboxes — for example restrict the merge to guest records, or require e-mail plus another matching attribute — state the assumption and its source in the design, and add a spec scenario "Shared business mailbox: records are not merged" with a test in task 1.1.
findings.title: The merge key rests on an assumption the design's own context contradicts

findings.location: design.md#Decision: Customers are merged by e-mail
findings.recommendation: The job deletes customer records nightly and unattended, and the plan gives no rollback, backup, audit trail, dry run or staged rollout. A wrong merge (see R-skeptic-1) cannot be undone: the deleted records' names, billing addresses and the original order-to-customer link are lost, and the spec says nothing about what happens to the fields of the records that are not kept. Add a way back — e.g. keep a merge log mapping each removed record and its moved orders to the survivor, soft-delete or archive instead of delete, start with a dry-run report — and a task that verifies it (an un-merge test, or a test that the log allows restoring the original records).
findings.title: Deleting the merged records is irreversible, with no way back

findings.evidence: A nightly job SHALL merge customer records that share an e-mail address into the oldest one, moving their orders to it.
findings.recommendation: The only scenarios are "Two records, one e-mail" and "No duplicate". Nothing says what "share an e-mail address" means when the case differs (the design lower-cases, the requirement does not say so), nor what happens to records with an empty or missing e-mail — if guest records can lack one, grouping on it could merge every such guest into one record. Add scenarios for an e-mail differing only in case, and for records without an e-mail (left untouched), each covered by a test named in task 1.1.
findings.title: The spec covers only the happy path

findings.recommendation: The change adds a scheduled job ("A nightly job merges customers that share an e-mail address.") that deletes data unattended, yet `operations` is unticked with no reason, so nobody reviews how the job is scheduled, observed, turned off or rolled back. Tick `operations`, or give the reason on its line.
findings.title: The new nightly job leaves the operations domain unticked
